question: What type of infectious agent is responsible for Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease?
explanation: Prions are protein particles that lack genetic material but cause brain tissue to degenerate. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h1)

question: Why does brain tissue take on a sponge-like appearance in this disease?

options.D: Formation of tiny holes from protein deposits

explanation: The buildup of rogue proteins causes brain cells to die, leaving tiny holes that make the tissue look like a sponge. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h1)

question: How do abnormal prions multiply in the central nervous system?

options.A: By forcing normal proteins to change their shape
options.B: By copying their own viral RNA
options.C: By absorbing nutrients from brain cells

explanation: Prions spread by physically changing normal healthy proteins into the abnormal shape. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h2)

question: What happens after normal host proteins are structurally converted?

options.A: They return to normal on their own
options.B: They are safely cleared by the body
options.D: They clump together to form harmful deposits

explanation: Once changed, these proteins stick together in clumps that damage the surrounding cells. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h2)

question: Which type of Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease happens spontaneously without any known cause?
explanation: Sporadic CJD is the most common form and occurs randomly for reasons doctors do not fully understand yet. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h3)

question: How is iatrogenic transmission of the disease usually acquired?

options.A: Through contaminated medical equipment or tissue

explanation: Iatrogenic cases happen when a patient accidentally comes into contact with infected material during a medical procedure. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h3)

question: Which involuntary physical sign is a classic feature of mid-stage disease?
explanation: Myoclonus refers to brief, shock-like muscle jerks that often appear as the illness progresses. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h4)

question: What condition is most common in a patient in the final stages of the disease?
explanation: Late-stage patients eventually become completely still, unresponsive, and unable to speak, a state called akinetic mutism. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h4)

question: Which procedure gives a definitive, 100% confirmation of the disease?
explanation: Only direct examination of brain tissue, usually after death or via biopsy, can definitively confirm the diagnosis. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h5)

question: Which imaging scan is most useful for spotting brain changes related to this condition?
explanation: An MRI scan helps doctors see specific patterns of damage in the brain tissue. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h5)

question: What is the main focus of nursing care for this condition?

options.D: Reversing protein damage in the brain

explanation: Because there is no cure, nursing care focuses entirely on keeping the patient comfortable and maintaining their dignity. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h6)

question: Why is careful skin care especially important for bedridden patients?

options.B: Patients are prone to severe rashes
options.C: Immobility puts them at high risk for pressure ulcers
options.D: Prions can spread through the skin

explanation: Patients who cannot move on their own need regular repositioning to prevent painful bedsores. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h6)

question: Why are standard hospital cleaning methods often useless against prions?

options.C: Prions resist normal heat and chemical disinfectants

explanation: Prions have tough physical properties that allow them to survive standard hospital cleaning and sterilization. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h7)

question: What is usually done with surgical tools used on a confirmed patient?
explanation: Because normal cleaning fails, contaminated instruments are often burned or treated with extreme chemical and heat protocols. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h7)

question: What is the typical life expectancy after symptoms start?
explanation: The disease moves very quickly, and most patients pass away within a year of showing symptoms. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h8)

question: How can nurses best help the family of a patient with this disease?

options.B: Connect them with counseling and support groups
options.D: Teach them how to do physical assessments

explanation: Families deal with intense emotional stress, making professional support and counseling vital parts of the care plan. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T5#GNS222_U4_T5_h8)
